messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Three years ago, Marcus Hayes was trapped in the flooded berthing compartment of his cruiser when Category 4 winds breached the hull. Water surged past his knees, then his chest, as forty sailors pressed together in a panic. The only way out was a narrow, pitch-black corridor, and the thick stench of ruptured liquor lockers mixed with the damp air, creating a suffocating, disorienting wall. He never forgot the exact spatial layout of that crush, the way the alcohol fumes burned his throat, or the terrifying density of bodies shifting in the dark. Now, as a Lieutenant navigating the bustling corridors of the naval base, those same stimuli instantly hijack him. When he walks past a crowded mess hall or catches the faint whiff of cheap whiskey on a colleague’s breath, his mind immediately flashes to the images of the rising water and the bulkhead buckling, the sensory details sharpening into a vivid, uncontrollable replay that leaves him gasping on the spot. These sudden sensory invasions rapidly convince him that his previous joy is permanently gone, that he no longer belongs in the civilian world, and that he is fundamentally isolated from everyone around him. Because he has come to believe he is irreparably broken and set apart from normal life, his nervous system permanently maps danger to those exact doorways and scent profiles, making him fixate on spatial layouts as if they are actively hunting him. Once he accepts this devastating self-assessment, the traumatic memories stop feeling like fleeting intrusions and instead solidify into a heavy, inescapable reality he feels he must endure to make sense of his new existence. The relentless mental reliving of the drowning crowd continuously confirms his growing conviction that he is irrevocably miserable and disconnected from his past self. Because he feels his body locked in those original trapped positions every time a memory surfaces, his nervous system permanently maps danger to open spaces and alcohol scent, ensuring that any proximity to crowds or liquor instantly pulls the memory forward. When the visceral feeling of being trapped overwhelms him, he instinctively cuts off contact with his friends and retreats into the darkened storage areas of the barracks, punishing himself for surviving. His deliberate isolation and self-imposed darkness actually fuel the intensity of the reenactments, making the visual memories sharper and more inescapable, while his avoidance of light and cutting of ties creates a vacuum where any unavoidable sound of a crowded deck or faint whiskey tang becomes overwhelmingly alarming. These avoidance habits and memory reinforcements have slowly hardened into a relentless loop over the past two years, draining his marriage and costing him a promotion. He has come to believe he deserves the suffering, so he stays in the shadows, convinced that happiness is a foreign country he can never return to. The final straw came during a base-wide emergency drill; the sudden alarm and sudden crush of personnel triggered a full bodily reenactment that left him unable to move or breathe, forcing his wife to intervene. Marcus finally walked into the clinic hoping for a way to stop the suffocating cycle, though he remains terrified that stepping into the light will simply confirm he no longer belongs anywhere.
